– the failing test (signature + snippet),

– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis

Details: The current bug report highlights that when encoding an empty byte array (new byte[0]), the Base64.encode method does not return an empty array but instead returns a CRLF sequence. This occurs despite the logical expectation that encoding empty input should produce empty output.

Analyzing the code reveals that Base64.encode(byte[]) calls encodeBase64(byte[], boolean, boolean) with arguments that eventually trigger the following code path: in encodeBase64, there is an early check `if (binaryData == null || binaryData.length == 0) return binaryData;` which means it should return the empty input array immediately. However, the bug report indicates the returned result contains CRLF instead, pointing to a suspicious mismatch between the documented code and actual behavior.

The failing test Base64InputStreamTest.testBase64EmptyInputStream() tests encoding and decoding empty byte arrays byte-by-byte by calling testByteByByte with an empty encoded array and empty decoded array, chunk size 76, and CRLF separator. The test expects that encoding empty input produces empty output, consistent with the early return in encodeBase64.

The discrepancy suggests that the problem may lie in how Base64InputStream encodes empty input streams, or how the chunking with CRLF line separators is handled. The problem report says Base64.encode on a zero-length array returns CRLF, implying that the chunking logic inadvertently adds a separator when it should not.

The code for Base64.encodeBase64 (lines 682-715) shows that it creates an internal Base64 instance and sets an internal buffer sized based on input length calculations. The Base64.encode() method is called with input data. This encoding process may add chunk separators such as CRLF when chunking is enabled, even if the input is empty. This would explain the observed behavior.

In summary, the encoded output for an empty array should be empty, but due to the chunking logic in Base64 encoding (especially when CRLF separators are specified), the method may wrongly produce a CRLF string. This violates the expectation tested by testBase64EmptyInputStream, causing test failure.

Thus, the root cause is that the chunking logic in the Base64 encoder erroneously inserts chunk separators (like CRLF) on empty input instead of returning an empty array. The test fails because it expects truly empty output on empty input, but gets CRLF instead. The fix should involve adjusting the chunking or encoding logic to prevent chunk separators being added when there is no data to encode.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
